section: bike-sharing system , the shared electric bicycle (SEB) is experiencing explosive growth in China as an emerging shared transportation mode. While shared transportation has long been linked to energy conservation and reducing emissions, a major problem facing SEB is whether it can reach the goal of greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction. This paper aims to evaluate GHG emissions at each stage of production, operation, and disposal of the SEB using life cycle assessment of GHG emissions. We also compared the differences in GHG emissions between the recycling incin- eration scenario (H1) and the recycling degradation scenario (H2) in the disposal stage. The GHG emissions of SEB in the production and operation stages were found to be 379.6173 kg CO 2 -eq and 183.4663 kg CO 2 -eq, respectively. However, the GHG emission reduction in the use stage was 1049.8374 kg CO 2 -eq. Thus, the net GHG reduction in the life cycle of the SEB was 487.3923 kg CO 2 -eq. (H1) and 433.9215 kg CO 2 -eq. (H2), respectively, indicating that SEB had a green effect. Non-recyclable parts of SEB will take 48 years to degrade in land ﬁ lls in the H2 scenario. The GHG emission thresholds for SEB were further discussed. When the average daily turnover rate of SEB was less than 4 and its operation day was less than 479, SEB would not be able to achieve the goal of GHG reduction in the whole life cycle, with the riding statistics remaining unchanged. Finally, some advice for practical issues of electric bicycle sharing in energy conservation and GHG reduction were presented in response to the results. 1. Shared transportation is a green development model innovation that supports sus- tainable urban transformation ( Enochsson et al., 2021 ; Mi and Coffman, 2019 ). In recent years, shared electric bicycles (SEBs) have rapidly spread in many cities as an emerging green travel mode in China because of their advantage in speed, trip distance, and so forth ( Chen et al., 2020a ; Cherry et al., 2016 ). The number of SEBs increased signi ﬁ cantly in recent years, from 175,000 to 1,157,000 between 2017 and 2020 in China with a com- pound annual growth rate of 105.4 %. Electric bicycle sharing systems have become one of the fast-growing transportation modes in China and around the world including in Asia, North America, and Europe ( He et al., 2019 ). Numerous studies related to electric bicycle sharing in these regions have been conducted by re- searchers, such as the ﬁ rst SEB in North America ( Langford et al., 2013 ), user demand and system availability of SEB ( Ji et al., 2014 ), factors in ﬂ uencing the choice of SEB ( Campbell et al., 2016 ), health impacts and safety issues of electric bicycles ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Otero et al., 2018 ), and more. However, the production, operation, and disposal of SEBs generate GHG emissions from a whole life cycle perspective. The result brings the question, “ Can the SEB reach the goal of GHG reduction? ” The question is inevitable and needs to be addressed in the electric bicycle-sharing systems for the future. The modalities of shared mobility are often seen as promising options for sustainable transport. Examples include shared car, shared bicycle, and SEB. Many researchers have analyzed the various environmental im- pacts of car sharing, such as the impacts of car sharing on net GHG emis- sions as a result of changes in travel behavior ( Shaheen et al., 2020 ; Martin and Shaheen, 2008 ), the life cycle impacts of car sharing on energy use and GHG emissions ( Amatuni et al., 2020 ; Chen and Kockelman, 2016 ), the impact of mobility changes from car sharing on GHG reduction ( Baptista et al., 2014 ), and more. Car sharing has been reported to reduce car ownership and personal annual vehicle kilometers, and promote a shift to other modes of transportation, with the potential to reduce GHG emissions ( Arbeláez Vélez and Plepys, 2021 ; Namazu and Dowlatabadi, 2018 ). The emergence of shared bicycles provides new ideas for reducing GHG emissions and promoting urban sustainable travel ( De Chardon, 2019 ; Ma et al., 2018 ). Bicycle sharing reduces CO 2 emissions compared to the previous mode of transportation used by users ( Luo et al., 2019 ; D'Almeida et al., 2021 ). The bicycle-sharing program could improve air quality and increase sports activity rates ( Anderson, 2015 ). Also, space, time, and the modal shift of different transportation modes have important effects on the environmental bene ﬁ ts of shared bicycles ( Zhang and Mi, 2018 ; Wang et al., 2020 ). There are few studies on GHG emissions from SEB. Evaluating the environmental bene ﬁ ts of SEB in the use phase is the main direction, such as the cost and carbon bene ﬁ ts of the hybrid electric bicycle share system ( Wamburu et al., 2021 ), the impact of SEBs and elec- tric bicycles on achieving urban climate goals ( Elliot et al., 2018 ; Felipe- Falgas et al., 2022 ; McQueen et al., 2020 ), and more. These studies show that SEBs have the potential to help cities and regions achieve climate goals. On the contrary, some research results indicated that SEBs have a substitution effect on other transportation modes and emitted more CO 2 than the transportation mode being substituted ( Reck et al., 2022 ). Various tools, such as environmental impact assessment ( Ivanova et al., 2016 ) and strategic environmental assessment ( Zhang et al., 2021 ), can be used to examine environmental implications of various systems. MFA and IO are two of the most common quantitative approaches, such as projec- tions of economic bene ﬁ ts and GHG emissions of recycling systems ( Liu et al., 2020 ; Tam et al., 2018 ), assessment of the ecosystem impacts of water scarcity ( Feng et al., 2014 ), and more. As another prominent method, the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) model focuses on products and supply chains from cradle to grave ( Bishop et al., 2021 ). The different environmen- tal impacts at various stages such as raw material extraction, production, use, and ﬁ nal recycling can be analyzed based on a large amount of data in the life cycle by the LCA model ( Hellweg and Mila I Canals, 2014 ). The LCA model was used to assess the environmental impact of bicycles including classic bicycles ( Chen et al., 2020b ), shared bicycles ( Coelho and Almeida, 2015 ), and electric bicycles ( Li et al., 2014 ) to discover the main factors contributing to negative impacts. The whole life cycle of SEB includes various stages, such as manufac- ture, use, waste disposal, and daily management. All stages of life cycle of SEBs require resource and energy inputs. It would generate waste and GHG emissions and indicate the potentially huge negative environmental impacts ( Mao et al., 2021 ). Based on literature review, on the one hand, we discovered that none of these studies assessed the quantity of GHG emis- sions produced by SEB in terms of manufacture, operation, maintenance, and disposal over the life cycle. It may cause misconceptions about environ- mental effects of SEB. On the other hand, the key contributors to negative environmental impacts were not identi ﬁ ed in these studies, which is critical to sustainable development of SEB. Moreover, the impact of SEB on energy savings and GHG reduction has not been fully included in the accounting of resource consumption. The importance of SEB in energy conservation and GHG reduction should be discussed. Compared to other studies, the life cycle GHG emission accounting method is used to calculate GHG emissions from the production, operation, and disposal of the SEB. Data collection at all stages is the biggest dif ﬁ culty in LCA modeling. These data cover the stage of production, man- agement, and recycling. A variety of data sources are consulted, such as ﬁ eld survey data, consultancy studies, and literature. Therefore, both the theory and the data in this paper are sound. The net GHG reduction and the GHG emission thresholds can be calculated in the life cycle by investi- gating the use of the SEB. The results can be expected to provide emission factors for SEB, which are necessary information to support system analysis of urban transportation sustainability. Finally, several policies and gover- nance proposals will be provided for the production design, market man- agement, and recycling of the SEB to achieve energy savings and GHG reduction goals, which may be bene ﬁ cial in improving the environmental contributions of SEB. 2. Materials and methods The LCA analysis is carried out in accordance with ISO 14067:2018 re- quirements and methodology to determine GHG emissions throughout the life cycle of a product, including raw material acquisition, material produc- tion, manufacturing, assembly, use, and disposal (reuse, recycling, inciner- ation, or land ﬁ ll). The four steps of LCA, as de ﬁ ned by ISO rules, are Goal and Scope De ﬁ nition, Inventory Analysis, Impact Assessment, and Results Interpretation ( ISO, 1997 ). The ﬁ rst step in the LCA is the Goal and Scope De ﬁ nition, which clari ﬁ es the questions to be answered in the LCA. It con- trols the scope and depth of the research. The next important phase in LCA is Life Cycle Inventory (LCI) Analysis, which collects, compiles, and quan- ti ﬁ es the inputs and outputs of the research object ( Lu et al., 2020 ). The daily transit, recycling, use stage, and every stage of manufacture are all tracked and built into the inventory data using the Inventory Analysis. The Impact Assessment is the third step of the LCA, which is inseparable from LCI. The Impact Assessment evaluates environmental impact of each stage using a database according to the Inventory Analysis results. It will provide information for the next stage (the Results Interpretation). The Re- sults Interpretation is the last step of LCA, under the content of the Goal and Scope De ﬁ nition. It identi ﬁ es the key issues that have a signi ﬁ cant environ- mental impact by conducting a thorough examination of the ﬁ ndings from the Life Cycle Inventory and the Impact Assessment. The limitations of this study and useful advice were also discussed. 2.1. De ﬁ nition of goals and scope The LCA model and PAS 2050 GHG emissions accounting methods are used to analyze the GHG emissions of the SEB in China. The environmental impact of SEB is assessed from a life cycle perspective. The entire life cycle includes the extraction of resources, preparation of the raw materials, prod- uct assembly, shipping, use, upkeep, and recovery of waste. Z. Zhu, C. Since 2017, there have been more than ten kinds of SEBs related to eight brands on the market, such as Meituan, Qingju, Hello, Songguo and Xiaoliu. Bicycle-sharing giants Meituan and Qingju, both of which use lead-acid batteries, accounted for nearly 63.3 % of the market share in China ( Leadleo, 2021 ). Therefore, the LCA model of electric bicycle sharing system is established based on the operation of Meituan SEB, which in- cludes user data from 256 cities in China. 2.1.1. The characteristics of electric bicycle sharing SEBs are now entering people's lives as a new shared transportation mode for the 3 - 10 km travel market due to the wide application of new technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), Arti ﬁ cial Intelligence (AI), and Big Data. There are great differences in different cities in terms of market access standards and quantity limits for the SEB. Before 2018, there was a lack of uni ﬁ ed product standards for electric bicycles. Some metropolises in China, such as Beijing and Shanghai discour- aged the development of the SEB due to concerns about travel safety, city image, and traf ﬁ c congestion. With the implementation of the Safety Tech- nical Speci ﬁ cation for Electric Bicycle (GB17761-2018) in 2019 ( Fig. 1 ), there are new development opportunities for SEB in China. The users of SEB are mainly in third-tier and fourth-tier cities because of the in ﬂ uence of policies and technologies. Compared with other traf ﬁ c tools, it was gen- erally believed that the SEB was safer for users. 58.7 % of users hold a pos- itive attitude towards the future development of SEB ( Iimedia, 2020 ). 2.1.2. Functional unit and system boundary The life cycle analysis approach is used to examine key aspects of energy consumption of SEB. The functional unit chosen is transporting one passenger for one kilometer by a SEB (i.e., p·km). The SEB service period is three years ( SPIR, 2020 ). The entire life cycle of the SEB can be separated into three stages: production, use, and disposal. The steps are divided into four sections such as the production section, alternative section, operation section, and dis- posal section. Energy used to manufacture SEB occurs in the production sec- tion. The operation section consumes energy to dispatch and maintain SEB. The disposal section generates energy consumption for the disposal of SEB. All processes involve energy consumption. However, the SEB saves energy by replacing other transportation modes during the alternative section. It involves energy savings as shown in Fig. 2 . The system boundary is the GHG generated by the input of each component into the assembly plant to SEB recycling, according to the data availability and continuity. It includes GHG emissions from materials, water, power, gas, and oil used in SEB manufacturing, transportation, maintenance, and recycling. 2.2. Impact assessment method 2.2.1. Applying GHG accounting methods to the production stage The SEB production process consists of four major steps: raw material processing, frame spraying, assembly, and transportation. Energy consump- tion of raw material processing occupies the main part of all energy con- sumption in the production process. GHG emissions of various raw materials can be calculated using the “ PAS 2050:2011 for the Evaluation of Greenhouse Gas Emissions of Goods and Services in the Life Cycle ” standard 1 and the China Products Carbon Footprint Factors Database (CPCD). 2 The following is the formula for calculating GHG emissions in the production process: PPE ¼ X n 1 EC n  EF n ð 1 Þ PPE : GHG emissions in the production process. EC n : the nth energy con- sumption in the production process. EF n : GHG emission factor for the nth en- ergy consumed in the production process. 2.2.2. Determining the types and sources of GHG emission factors The object of this research was the electric bicycle-sharing industry in China, represented by Meituan SEB. The basic parameters in the calculation were determined using the above GHG calculation methods. GHG account- ing was performed at three stages during the life cycle. Finally, GHG conser- vation thresholds were obtained. Table 1 lists the types and sources of vehicle GHG emission factors. 3.2. GHG emissions in the production stage SEB companies typically contract out production to conventional elec- tric bicycle factories. The SEB can be treated as an ordinary electric bicycle. Electric bicycle components manufacturing primarily comprises creating all spare parts and auxiliary materials. Two components make up the majority of the SEB: the bicycle system and the technical product system (such as chips). The technical product system is often light in weight and recyclable. Therefore, only the material and energy usage of the SEB is taken into ac- count at the production stage. Material and energy usage in the SEB production stage was collected from electric bicycle manufacturers, distributors, and some research. Through electric bicycle manufacturers and distributors, the SEB weighed about 51.100 kg, including 13.522 kg of steel and copper, 17.310 kg of alu- minum alloys, 3.210 kg of plastic, 3.500 kg of rubber, 11.700 kg of lead alloys 5 , 0.060 kg paper, etc. 0.0026 m 3 of water, 0.9639 kW·h of electricity, and 2.2143 m 3 of natural gas were all used to produce a SEB. GHG emissions in the use stage The data in the use stage of SEB included energy consumption data ob- tained from Meituan and the CPCD database. User behavior data was pro- vided by a questionnaire survey that covered 256 cities in China. The average distance SEB traveled per trip was 3.06 km. The power consump- tion per kilometer was 0.014 kW·h. The daily turnover rate was between six and ten. According to the Technical Requirements for Chargers for Elec- tric Bicycles (GBT36944-2018) 6 released by the SAMR of China, the actual power consumption per kilometer of the SEB is 0.0169 kW·h due to the loss in the charging process 7 . It was assumed that the daily turnover rate of the SEB was eight. Therefore, the average daily distance of the SEB was 24.48 km. We found that SEB could replace 11 kinds of transportation modes in- cluding buses, cars, metros, etc. from the questionnaire. Fig. 3 shows that buses are the transportation modes with the largest proportion replaced by the SEB. SEB mainly replaced the transportation modes that produced GHG, indicating that it had the effect of reducing GHG emissions. Fig. 4 shows the GHG emission factors of different transportation modes in the use stage. According to the calculation method of GHG emissions, when the SEB traveled 1 km, it would reduce 39.2 g of GHG emissions, showing that SEB was a green product. Finally, we could calculate that total GHG re- ductions during the use stage of SEB were 1049.8374 kg CO 2 -eq. 3.4. GHG emissions in the operation and dispatch stage Energy consumption data in the maintenance stage of the SEB was col- lected from interviews with the staff of Meituan SEB. As the service time went by, SEB would require approximately seven maintenance over the lifetime. After the 7th restoration, the severity of damage to SEB would be considerably worsened, and usually beyond repair. It was calcu- lated that the GHG emissions in the maintenance stage of the SEB were 5.5288 kg CO 2 -eq in the whole life cycle according to the calculation method of GHG emissions. It is a big issue when SEBs park illegally. SEB companies employ dis- patch vans to transport and redistribute SEBs to maintain a good city image. It mainly relies on manual handling and transportation, which is divided by region and carried out in 24-h shifts. Small trucks and electric three-wheelers are the primary dispatch vehicles, which are similar to the general cargo transport system. GHG emissions in the disposal stage Energy consumption data in the disposal stage were obtained from the EFBD database. The disposal consists of two scenarios: recycling incinera- tion and recycling degradation. The recyclable parts of SEB were recycled by the renewable resource recycling enterprise, including frames, electric motors, battery units, and other metal parts. The non-recyclable parts mainly included 3.50 kg of rubber, 3.21 kg of plastic, and 0.06 kg of paper. We assumed that technical products, such as electronic chips, could be completely recycled and repurposed. According to the Principle of Land ﬁ ll Site Selection (CJJ17-2004) 10 , the distance between the land ﬁ ll site and the urban planning built-up area should be greater than 5.00 km, and the distance from residential areas should be longer than 500 m. At present, there is no uniform regulation on the distance between waste incin- eration plants and renewable resource recycling plants in urban living areas. It will be ultimately determined by “ environmental impact assess- ment ” of the project. Shenyang was taken as an observation area because of its good opera- tion of SEB. There are three waste incineration plants in Shenyang and more than 110 renewable resource recycling plants. The map software was used to measure the distance of waste incineration plants from urban residential areas and the distance of renewable resource recycling plants from urban areas. The average of the distances was calculated to be 28.93 km and 1.00 km, respectively. Therefore, it was assumed that the dis- tance from urban area to renewable resource recycling plant was 1.00 km, the distance from renewable resource recycling plant to waste incineration plant was 27.93 km, and the distance from the renewable resource recycling plant to the land ﬁ ll was 4.00 km. 1) In the recycling incineration scenario, diesel vehicles could transport 100 SEBs from urban area to a re- newable resource recycling plant 1.00 km away for recycling. Then, non- recyclable parts as municipal solid waste including rubber, plastic, and paper were transported to a waste incineration plant 27.93 km away for in- cineration. The average transportation distance of SEB was 0.047 km. It would reduce a total of 0.6385 kg CO 2 -eq in the recycling incineration sce- nario according to the GHG emission calculation method. 2) In the recycling degradation scenario, non-recyclable parts were transported by diesel vehicles to a land ﬁ ll site 4.00 km away. The average transportation distance of the SEB was 0.015 km. We found that the SEB would produce 52.8323 kg CO 2 -eq of GHG emissions according to the GHG emission calcu- lation method in Scenario 2. SEB operators were asked to increase the amount of SEBs in the future by 59 % of the users. Therefore, there would be a huge market demand for SEB ( Leadleo, 2021 ). It resulted in a maximum GHG reduction of 419.157 kt CO 2 -eq ac- cording to the life cycle GHG emission accounting method in 2021. Discussions This paper innovatively calculates the GHG emissions of SEB from pro- duction, operation and dispatch to disposal, and calculates the GHG emis- sion reduction in the use stage. It was found that SEBs are green products in the life cycle. Scenario 1 is the one with the best environmental bene ﬁ ts. The production stage has the largest impact on GHG emissions at about 62 %, and the operation and dispatch stage accounts for about 30 % of total GHG emissions in scenario 1. 98 % of energy consumption during the pro- duction stage was consumed by GHG emissions from raw materials. By fur- ther analyzing the materials input at the production stage, we ﬁ nd that the use of aluminum alloys has caused the maximum negative environmental impact. This is mainly because aluminum production mainly relies on the electrolytic method, which consumes a lot of electricity. If more environ- mentally friendly materials, such as composite materials, are used in pro- duction instead of aluminum alloys, the GHG emissions of SEBs will be greatly reduced. Although we collected all kinds of components of SEB and made various assumptions, it may cause some errors in the calculation results due to the use of different types of materials in the production stage, such as glass ﬁ bers, photographic materials, and copper in electronic sys- tems. In addition, since the content of a single emission factor database could not meet the requirements of the paper, we had to refer to several da- tabases and some research results. Although we have carefully identi ﬁ ed emission factors for each material, the multiple sources of emission factors may introduce some uncertainty in the results. The replacement rate of SEBs for high-emission transportation modes determines the emission re- duction effect in the use stage. Due to the lack of a complete and effective recycling system, we were unable to assess the GHG emission reduction generated during the recycling process of SEB, which is crucial to enhance the environmental bene ﬁ ts of SEB. Therefore, it can be considered that op- timizing SEB production, encouraging green travel, and establishing a recycling system may be the future direction of green development of SEB. Promoting SEB to replace high-emission transportation modes It was found that SEB had a substitution effect on other transportation modes and could result in an effective reduction of GHG emissions. How- ever, SEB mainly replaced low-GHG emissions or zero-GHG emissions transportation modes such as walking, buses, and shared bicycles, which accounted for 69.5 %. The replacement rate for high-GHG emissions trans- portation modes such as private cars and taxis was low. Therefore, promot- ing SEB to replace high-GHG emission transportation modes is one of the important ways to reduce more GHG emissions. It was shown that the aver- age single trip distance of the SEB was 3.06 km. The travel distance of high- GHG emissions transportation modes is mainly concentrated in 8 - 20 km. Increasing the trip distance of SEB is the key to replacing high-emission transportation modes. Cities with SEBs can plan to develop slow traf ﬁ c sys- tems, set up dedicated lanes for SEBs, improve road signs and traf ﬁ c mark- ings, and remove traf ﬁ c barriers. It is necessary to plan the parking areas for SEBs to solve the problem of hindering traf ﬁ c by parking indiscriminately. Finally, green travel should be actively promoted. SEB companies should improve their operation level to increase their market share of SEBs. These measures will ensure that the SEBs are fully charged and trouble- free to improve the user experience. 5.2. Determining the number of SEBs according to the capacity of the market Currently, there are more than ten kinds of SEBs under eight brands in the China market where competition among SEB operators is ﬁ erce. SEB operators are trying to gain customer loyalty by increasing the number of SEBs to increase their market share and gain suf ﬁ cient pro ﬁ ts. However, SEB operators only pay attention to economic bene ﬁ ts in the process of attracting users. The increase in the number of SEBs will lead to a gradual increase in the ratio of empty SEBs, which will affect GHG emission thresh- olds of SEB and reduce the environmental bene ﬁ ts. If there is no scienti ﬁ c plan for the ef ﬁ ciency and amount of SEBs, it will be dif ﬁ cult for SEB to achieve energy conservation and GHG reduction. The government can ad- vocate SEB companies to account for GHG emission reductions. According to the market demand and urban traf ﬁ c conditions, it is necessary to pro- mote a quota for the number of SEBs to achieve control of the number of SEBs of various SEB companies. SEB companies should change their busi- ness strategies and focus on how to improve the quality of service, improve energy saving and emission reduction, continuously improve the user expe- rience and enhance the social image. 5.3. Improving the disposal stage of the SEB to create a circular industrial chain Electric bicycle-sharing should be considered a green product. A com- prehensive and ef ﬁ cient recycling system for SEB is absent currently. Pri- vate institutions remain essential to the recycling of the SEB. The lack of a consistent recycling system results in inef ﬁ ciency and waste. As a result, the recycling market for SEB is not active ( MOC, 2020 ) and, the lack of a complete recycling system made it impossible to calculate the deduction ef- fect of the recycling process in this LCA calculation. More ef ﬁ cient electric bicycle sharing recycling businesses will considerably reduce environmen- tal consequences at the production stage from a life cycle perspective. The government should improve the policy system design, such as the extension of producer responsibility system and recovery compensation system. It is necessary to promote cooperation between recycling companies and SEB companies, which is conducive to the ﬁ xed-point recovery and centralized disposal of abandoned SEBs. It is effective for recycling SEBs by establishing new recycling processing models and recycling platforms, which need the support of information technology, such as big data, blockchain, and arti ﬁ - cial intelligence. In addition, we should also promote the business linkage of production enterprises, operating enterprises, recycling enterprises, and waste treatment enterprises based on the life cycle to build a SEB recycling system. Finally, waste battery treatment technology should be fo- cused on to improve the recycling level and pollution prevention capacity of the waste battery recycling industry. 6. Conclusion Transportation is the backbone of the national economy and society in China. GHG emission reduction in transportation has become an important area in the country. Shared transportation is a new way to reduce emis- sions. SEB has become a new green shared transportation mode after public bicycles and shared bicycles. The life cycle analysis approach was used in this study to analyze the factors and main parameters that affect the energy consumption of SEB. The life cycle GHG emissions accounting model for SEB was established based on the obtained factors and parameters. Meituan SEB, the most common type of electric bicycle sharing, was chosen as the object of the current research. This study evaluated resource consumption and GHG emissions in each stage of production, operation, and disposal of the SEB. The differences in GHG emissions between the recycling incineration sce- nario and recycling degradation scenario were compared in the disposal stage. Moreover, net GHG emissions in the whole life cycle of the SEB were calculated separately under different disposal scenarios. GHG emis- sion thresholds of the SEB were analyzed in terms of operating days and daily turnover rates. Finally, we found that the GHG emissions in the pro- duction and operation stages were 379.6173 kg CO 2 -eq and 183.4663 kg CO 2 -eq respectively. GHG emission reduction in the use stage was 1049.8374 kg CO 2 -eq in the whole life cycle. GHG emissions differed greatly between the two different disposal scenarios. GHG reductions of SEB were 0.6385 kg CO 2 -eq in the recycling incineration scenario. GHG emissions of SEB were 52.8323 kg CO 2 -eq in the recycling degradation sce- nario. Therefore, net GHG reductions in the life cycle of the SEB were 487.3923 kg CO 2 -eq (Scenario 1) and 433.9215 kg CO 2 -eq (Scenario 2). It was indicated that SEB might be a green product. If a SEB was deposited in a land ﬁ ll, it would take 48 years to degrade. The ﬁ nal calculation showed that if the daily average turnover rates were less than 4 and the operating days were less than 479, the SEB would not be able to achieve the goal of GHG reduction in the whole life cycle. Although this study comprehensively evaluates the GHG emission im- pact of each stage of SEB, several important future research topics could be studied to enhance the existing research, such as optimizing SEB produc- tion, encouraging green travel, and establishing a recycling system. Shared economy is very important to the sustainable development of society. In the future, the role of many products in the shared economy, such as transpor- tation, logistics and express delivery, and life service, still needs to be ex- plored more thoroughly to achieve the sustainable development of society.
